questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of fixed costs?
options: Costs that do not change as output changes in the short run
Costs that change directly with output
Costs that never change at all
The total costs of a business
questions.why: Fixed means fixed with respect to OUTPUT. Rent, insurance and salaries are paid whether you produce one unit or a thousand.
whyNot: Those are variable costs.
Rent can rise; it just does not rise because output rose. Fixed refers to the relationship with output.
Total costs are fixed plus variable.

questions.stem: A business sells 3,000 units at $14 each. What is sales revenue?
questions.why: Sales revenue = volume x price = 3,000 x $14 = $42,000.
whyNot: This appears to use $7 rather than $14. Check the price.
This adds the two figures. Revenue is a product, not a sum.
This is ten times too small.

questions.stem: Fixed costs are $9,000 and variable costs are $3 per unit. At 2,000 units, what are total costs?
whyNot: This adds the variable cost PER UNIT to fixed costs without multiplying by output.
This appears to use 1,000 units. Check the output figure.
That is total variable costs on their own. Fixed costs still have to be added.

questions.stem: Total costs are $15,000 at an output of 2,000 units. What is average cost?
questions.why: Average cost = total costs / output = 15,000 / 2,000 = $7.50 per unit.
whyNot: This multiplies instead of dividing.
This subtracts output from total costs, which has no meaning.
This divides output by total costs, the wrong way round.

questions.stem: Why does average cost fall as output rises?
options: Fixed costs are spread over more units, so fixed cost per unit falls
Variable cost per unit falls automatically
Total fixed costs fall as output rises
Selling price rises with output
questions.why: Total fixed costs stay the same while output rises, so each unit carries a smaller share of them. Variable cost per unit is unchanged. This is the mechanism behind economies of scale.
whyNot: Variable cost per unit normally stays the same, though bulk buying can reduce it.
Total fixed costs do not change with output. It is the cost PER UNIT that falls.
Price is a separate decision and is not driven by output.

questions.stem: A bakery has fixed costs of $3,000, variable costs of $0.80 a loaf and sells at $2.50. What is profit at 2,000 loaves?
whyNot: That is total revenue. Costs still have to be deducted.
This deducts only the variable costs and forgets the $3,000 of fixed costs.
That is total variable costs, not profit.

questions.stem: The same bakery doubles output to 4,000 loaves. Profit rises from $400 to $3,800. Why does profit rise by so much more than output?
options: The $3,000 of fixed costs was already being paid, so all the extra contribution is profit
Variable costs fall to zero at higher output
The selling price rises when output doubles
Fixed costs double as well
questions.why: Once fixed costs are covered, each additional loaf adds its full contribution of $1.70 to profit. Doubling output added 2,000 x $1.70 = $3,400 with no extra fixed cost at all.
whyNot: Variable costs double with output; they do not disappear.
Price is unchanged at $2.50 in the example.
Fixed costs stay at $3,000, which is precisely why profit rises so sharply.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a semi-variable cost?
options: A phone contract with a standing charge plus usage charges
Rent on a factory
Raw materials
Business insurance
questions.why: A semi-variable cost has a fixed element and a variable element. The standing charge is fixed; the usage varies with activity.
whyNot: Rent is purely fixed.
Raw materials are purely variable.
Insurance is purely fixed.

questions.stem: Which of the following would raise sales revenue for a product with price inelastic demand?
options: Raising the price
Lowering the price
Reducing output
Increasing variable costs
questions.why: With inelastic demand the percentage fall in quantity is smaller than the percentage rise in price, so revenue rises. This links directly to PED in WBS11 topic 1.3.2.4.
whyNot: Lowering price raises revenue when demand is ELASTIC, not inelastic.
Less output sold means less revenue.
Costs do not affect revenue at all; revenue is price times quantity.

questions.stem: Why does a guesthouse with very low variable costs discount heavily for late bookings?
options: An empty room earns nothing, and a discounted booking still adds most of its price as contribution
Variable costs rise sharply with occupancy
Discounting reduces fixed costs
Empty rooms cost more than occupied ones
questions.why: With a variable cost of around $12 on a $95 rate, a room sold at even $40 still adds $28 of contribution towards fixed costs. Unsold, it adds nothing. That cost structure explains the whole pricing behaviour of the sector.
whyNot: They are low and stay low: breakfast, laundry and water.
Fixed costs are unaffected by pricing decisions.
An empty room costs slightly less, and earns nothing at all.
